newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW -Japan November current account data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -Japan November current account data.

text.p: The following is a selection of analysts' reactions to Japan's current account data for November, which showed a year-on-year fall of 15.4 percent to 664.1 billion yen.
JESPER KOLL, HEAD OF RESEARCH, J.P. MORGAN
"It's a little bit better that than what the market was looking for and better for Japan in that the external surplus is still coming down compared to a year ago."

"But you find that the trade surplus is basically flat compared to a year ago and what is depressing the overall current account numbers is the fact that the weak yen is decreasing investment income of Japanese portfolio investment and of Japanese operations overseas."
AKIYOSHI TAKUMORI, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SAKURA SECURITIES
"The current account surplus is less than what I had expected as I had been eyeing a figure of about 777 billion yen. It shows that the decreasing trend for the current account is still intact."

"But looking at the trade data for the first 20 days of December, it shows that the pace of decrease for the trade surplus is slowing down. The yen's depreciation has had an effect in lifting Japanese exports.
"Taking this into account, the drop in the current account surplus is due to a large deficit in the services."
YASUJI YAMANAKI, VICE PRESIDENT, BANK OF AMERICA
"These figures won't really have much of an impact on the currency market, because they are not so extreme.

"There's the chance that the continuing weakness of the yen will bring us to a point in several months where the decline of the surplus may slow or come to a halt. If this happens, it's hard to know what sort of comments or response we can expect from the U.S. This is something we have to be cautious about, particularly in the currency market."

"Obviously this process of trade adjustment is taking longer than expected. We expect an increase in the current account surplus in calendar 1997 and it's only a matter of time. The yen continues to be weak so this should help the surplus rise. It should turn around sometime in early '97."
